narrative:
Your application was denied because the model estimated a 92% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a very high risk estimate, so the admissions decision treated your profile as much more likely than a typical applicant to lead to bar failure. Gender and race were not used in this prediction.

The strongest factor was your third-year class-standing decile: you were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the middle of their class. This was the most influential signal and pushed the prediction toward failure. Your LSAT score was the second most important factor: 26 is well below the accepted-student average of about 37, and it also pushed toward failure. Your first-year class-standing decile, also 1 compared with an accepted average of 6, was the third most important factor and reinforced the same direction. Together, these academic indicators outweighed other information in your profile.

To improve future applications, focus on the areas flagged. Prepare thoroughly for a higher LSAT score, consider additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates readiness for law study, and ask admissions offices for feedback. Applying to schools with holistic or conditional-admission pathways may also help. The score is a probability, not a certainty, but it should guide concrete academic strengthening before you reapply.
